title: PortKnock
summary: A tiny port-knocking daemon that hides SSH behind a secret sequence.
description: PortKnock is a single-binary daemon that keeps a firewall port closed until a client sends a pre-agreed sequence of connection attempts, then opens it just for that source IP for a short window. It was built to learn how netfilter and raw sockets actually work rather than to replace a real bastion host. The write-up covers why knock sequences are obscurity not security, how replay is mitigated with a rotating time-based secret, and what an attacker sniffing the wire can still recover. Ships with a systemd unit, a client CLI, and a test harness that fuzzes malformed packets.

title: CTF Forge
summary: Author, containerise, and host capture-the-flag challenges from one dashboard.
description: CTF Forge lets a committee run an internal capture-the-flag event without hand-rolling Docker files for every challenge. Authors describe a challenge in a small YAML spec — category, points, flag format, and the files to serve — and Forge builds an isolated container per team on demand, rotates per-team flags to kill flag-sharing, and streams a live scoreboard. Built for the club's beginner CTF nights, it deliberately sandboxes each challenge on its own network namespace so a pwnable can't reach the scoring API. The repo includes three example challenges (web, crypto, forensics) and a scoring model that rewards early solves.

title: DuckPass
summary: A browser extension that coaches you to a stronger password as you type.
description: DuckPass is a WebExtension that scores a password field live and, instead of just showing a red bar, explains what would actually make it harder to crack — length beats symbols, a passphrase beats l33t-speak, and reuse is the real killer. Everything runs locally: no keystroke ever leaves the browser, and the entropy estimate uses a small on-device wordlist rather than an API. It was the club's intro-to-extensions project, so the code is heavily commented and the README walks through the manifest v3 permissions model line by line. Works in Chrome and Firefox.

title: SigHunt
summary: Cluster unknown malware samples by behaviour to surface new families.
description: SigHunt takes a folder of sandbox reports and groups samples that behave alike — same registry keys touched, same network beacon shape, same file-drop pattern — so an analyst can triage a bucket of unknowns without a signature for each one. It uses TF-IDF over the API-call traces and agglomerative clustering, then renders a dendrogram you can cut at any threshold. Built as a machine-learning reading-group project, the notebook explains why clustering is honest triage and classification here would be over-claiming. Ships with a small labelled evaluation set and the confusion matrix that comes out of it.

title: Arcade Siege
summary: A pixel-art tower defense where the towers are firewall rules.
description: Arcade Siege is a browser tower-defense game with a security-club joke baked in: your towers are firewall rules, the creeps are packets, and a boss wave is a slow-loris that only a rate-limit tower can stop. It started as the club's Godot game-jam entry and grew a level editor, a wave designer, and a small original chiptune soundtrack. The point of shipping it in the showcase is that it runs entirely in the browser sandbox — the safest possible thing to host — which is exactly the kind of `web` release the showcase recommends first. Playable on desktop and mobile.

title: Packet Pigeon
summary: A pcap pretty-printer that turns a capture into a readable story.
description: Packet Pigeon reads a pcap and prints a plain-English timeline of a connection — the handshake, the TLS hello with its SNI, the requests, the resets — so a beginner can see what Wireshark is showing without learning every column first. It's a teaching tool, not a replacement for tshark, and the README says so. Built in Go for a single static binary, it decodes the common layers, redacts payloads by default, and can emit either coloured terminal output or Markdown for a report. The test suite runs against a handful of checked-in captures so behaviour is reproducible.

title: Roster Radar
summary: A phone app for checking members in at the door of an event.
description: Roster Radar is the app a committee member holds at the door: scan a member's QR, see their name and whether their DUSA membership is current, and tap to check them in — all against the club's own roster, never a third-party service. It caches the roster on device so the queue keeps moving when the venue Wi-Fi dies, then syncs check-ins back when it reconnects. Built with Expo so one codebase runs on both platforms, it was the club's intro-to-mobile project and leans hard on the offline-first pattern. No attendee data is stored beyond the event.

title: Byte Badge
summary: An open-hardware conference badge that boots into a CTF.
description: Byte Badge is a DIY electronic conference badge built around an ESP32 that boots into a tiny hardware-hacking CTF — solder the headers, flash the firmware, and the first challenge is figuring out the serial baud rate. The KiCad board files, a bill of materials that comes in under fifteen dollars, and the firmware are all open so a member can order their own from any fab. It's an early-stage idea rather than a finished run: the schematic is done and one prototype exists, and the repo is looking for contributors to design the next three challenges. Reached through its GitHub repo — there is no binary to download here.
